Chapter 6: Progressing Safely—Listening to Your Body and Advancing Gradually
As you start feeling stronger and more confident, you might catch yourself asking—when should I start making things a bit more challenging?
Progression is a huge part of any fitness journey. But for senior women, it’s really important to approach this next step with extra care. Your body is always sending you messages—sometimes in whispers, sometimes a bit louder—letting you know when it’s time to step up, and when it’s better to hold back.
Here’s the main idea: take it slow and steady. Instead of making big jumps in weight or intensity, try making small, manageable changes. Maybe you add just one or two extra repetitions to your favorite exercise, grab a slightly heavier can from the pantry, or hold a movement for a few seconds longer. The goal is to challenge yourself, but never to the point of feeling overwhelmed.
Think of your body like a beautiful musical instrument. You wouldn’t crank the strings of a violin all at once, right? You’d tune it gently, making tiny adjustments. Exercise is just like that. If you try a new movement or add resistance and it feels too tough—or you feel discomfort—that’s your cue to ease back and try again another day.
So, how can you progress safely? Here are a few practical ideas:
Try increasing repetitions or sets just a little—say, moving from eight up to ten reps. Or, swap out your usual weight for something just a bit heavier, or choose a resistance band with a bit more tension. You might also add a brand-new exercise to your routine, focusing on a muscle group you haven’t targeted before. And don’t forget—sometimes just holding a position for a few extra seconds can make a big difference!
Most importantly, listen closely to your body while you’re moving—and even after you’ve finished. There’s a big difference between normal muscle fatigue and actual pain. Feeling a bit of mild soreness after trying something new? That’s pretty common. But if you notice any sharp or lingering pain, that’s your body’s way of saying, “let’s pause and check in.” Remember, rest and recovery are just as crucial as the workouts themselves—they’re what help your muscles rebuild and grow stronger.
When you move forward at a pace that feels comfortable, and really tune in to your body’s feedback, strength training stays both safe and enjoyable. You’ll not only build your physical resilience—you’ll also build trust in your own judgement and abilities.
